title: Connect AI Agents to Fabric API for GraphQL with a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server
summary: A Microsoft Learn how-to tutorial that walks through standing up a local Node.js Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in front of a Fabric GraphQL endpoint, so AI agents such as GitHub Copilot or Cursor can discover a Fabric schema through introspection and translate natural-language questions into GraphQL queries — plus the service-principal auth setup, the two MCP tools the server exposes, and production security guidance.
audience: Application/integration developers and Fabric admins wiring AI coding assistants or agents into Fabric data, and architects evaluating GraphQL API as an AI-agent access surface rather than only a human-facing API.
why_it_matters: The existing GraphQL API source only mentions AI-agent/MCP access in a single sentence. This tutorial is the dedicated, mechanism-level source for that claim: it shows concretely what an MCP bridge to Fabric GraphQL requires (service principal auth, introspection enabled at the workspace level, a specific two-tool MCP server contract) and what Microsoft explicitly warns not to do in production, closing a single-source dependency gap on one of the article's more forward-looking claims.
takeaways: AI-agent access to Fabric GraphQL is not automatic — it requires a separate MCP server component acting as a translator between the agent and the GraphQL endpoint, authenticating with its own service principal identity.

Schema introspection, which is disabled by default in Fabric for security reasons, must be explicitly enabled by a workspace admin before an MCP server (and therefore an AI agent) can discover the schema at all.
The reference MCP server design is deliberately minimal: two tools (introspect-schema, query-graphql) rather than one hand-defined tool per GraphQL type or operation.

Microsoft explicitly scopes the published sample server to local development and lists concrete production hardening steps (Key Vault, authZ, audit logging, managed hosting, rate limiting, secret rotation) rather than treating it as production-ready as-is.

MCP itself is a vendor-neutral protocol (adopted by OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot Studio, and Microsoft Foundry), and GraphQL's self-describing schema is called out as a specific structural fit for it — this is a claim about protocol/format fit, not a Fabric-specific guarantee.

claims.text: Connecting an AI agent to Fabric's GraphQL API for natural-language querying requires deploying a separate local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that acts as a bridge/translator between the agent and the GraphQL endpoint, rather than the agent talking to the GraphQL endpoint directly.

The MCP server authenticates to Fabric using a dedicated service principal (an Azure App Registration with a client secret) rather than an interactive user sign-in, because it runs as an unattended background process that AI agents call automatically.

GraphQL schema introspection is disabled by default in Fabric for security reasons and must be explicitly enabled by a workspace admin before an MCP server or AI agent can discover the schema's types, fields, and relationships.

The reference GraphQL MCP server exposes exactly two tools to an AI agent: introspect-schema (retrieves the full schema, called first) and query-graphql (executes a GraphQL query/mutation with optional variables) — a single generic pair rather than one tool per GraphQL type or operation.

The typical GraphQL MCP workflow is schema discovery via introspection, query planning from the natural-language request against that schema, query generation, execution against the GraphQL endpoint, then response formatting back to the user — introspection is a required first step, not optional.

Enabling AI-agent access to Fabric GraphQL requires enabling service principals for Fabric APIs at the tenant level (a Fabric tenant-admin setting) in addition to granting that service principal workspace or GraphQL-item-level permissions, so the setup spans tenant admin, workspace admin, and app-registration owner roles.

Microsoft's published local GraphQL MCP server sample is explicitly scoped to development and learning use, using HTTP transport and .env-file secrets, and is not positioned as production-ready as published.

For a production GraphQL MCP deployment, Microsoft recommends storing secrets in Azure Key Vault instead of .env files, implementing authorization/network security/firewall rules, enabling audit logging for all GraphQL queries, hosting on Azure App Service or Container Instances, adding rate limiting and authentication on the MCP endpoints, and rotating client secrets and certificates regularly.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a vendor-neutral standard for connecting AI assistants to external systems and data, adopted by multiple major AI platforms including OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot Studio, and Microsoft Foundry, not a Fabric-specific or Microsoft-proprietary protocol.

GraphQL's self-describing, strongly-typed schema is cited as a structural fit for MCP integrations specifically because it lets an AI agent discover available data types, fields, and relationships through introspection rather than requiring a hand-written data-source description.
